title: Modular exponentiation: repeated multiplication vs square-and-multiply
problem_statement: Given integers a >= 0 and e >= 0, compute a^e mod m for the fixed modulus m = 2^64 - 59 (the largest prime below 2^64). By convention a^0 mod m = 1.

input.parameter: n = bit length of the exponent e (n = 0 for e = 0), so 2^(n-1) <= e < 2^n for n >= 1.
input.size_measure: n bits for e, plus one word for a (reduced mod m first) and the fixed 64-bit m. Every multiplication mod m costs O(1) word operations, so costs are counted in modular multiplications.

algorithms.name: repeated multiplication
algorithms.idea: Start from 1 and multiply by a (mod m) e times.
algorithms.pseudocode: r = 1; repeat e times: r = r * a mod m; return r
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(e) = Theta(2^n) multiplications mod m (exactly e of them, and e >= 2^(n-1) for e >= 1)
algorithms.space_complexity: O(n) bits besides the input: one word each for r and a, plus the loop counter of range(e), which has as many bits as e
algorithms.correctness: Invariant: after k iterations r = a^k mod m.

algorithms.name: left-to-right square-and-multiply (binary method)
algorithms.idea: Scan the bits of e from the most significant one; for each bit square the accumulator, and multiply it by a when the bit is 1.
algorithms.pseudocode: r = 1; for each bit b of e, most significant first: r = r * r mod m; if b = 1: r = r * a mod m; return r
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n) multiplications mod m: for e >= 1, n squarings plus one multiplication per 1-bit of e (at most n), and the conversion bin(e) of e to binary, linear in n under the machine-model assumption in background (e = 0 costs one squaring)
algorithms.space_complexity: O(n) bits (the exponent; the implementation also materialises its n-character binary string)
algorithms.correctness: Invariant: after processing the top j bits of e, whose value is k, r = a^k mod m; a further bit b gives a^(2k + b) = (a^k)^2 * a^b (Knuth 1997; proved in PROOFS.md, section 3).

relationship: Repeated multiplication is linear in the VALUE of e, hence exponential, Theta(2^n), in its bit length n. Square-and-multiply reuses the powers a^(2^i) by squaring and needs at most 2n multiplications for e >= 1: Theta(n), polynomial (linear) in the input size.

sources.title: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2: Seminumerical Algorithms (3rd ed.)

sources.authors: Rivest, R. L.; Shamir, A.; Adleman, L.
sources.title: A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems
sources.note: Background only: the RSA cryptosystem, whose encryption and decryption are modular exponentiations.

sources.title: New directions in cryptography
sources.note: Background only: key exchange by modular exponentiation.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with Python's built-in pow(a, e, m) (used only as the oracle) on random bases (including 0, 1, m - 1 and bases larger than m) and random exponents of bit length n = 0..16, 32, 64, 128, 1000 and 4096 (repeated multiplication up to n = 16). V2: on the worst-case exponents e = 2^n - 1 (all bits set) runtimes fit 2^n (n = 12..20) and n (n = 1000..64000). Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry (the primality of m and that no prime lies between m and 2^64, correctness, the exact counts e and n + popcount(e), space, the addition-chain lower bound and the factor-2 caveat) and names the deterministic tests that check each one.

lower_bounds.bound: at least ceil(log2 e) >= n - 1 multiplications (each multiplication at most doubles the largest exponent computed so far)
lower_bounds.setting: addition-chain (multiplication-only) model: each step multiplies two powers of a computed earlier

caveats: Bit-size view: n is the bit length of e. In the VALUE e, repeated multiplication is linear; it is exponential only in the input length. The fixed 64-bit modulus makes every multiplication O(1); for a k-bit modulus multiply both costs by the cost M(k) of one k-bit modular multiplication. Square-and-multiply is within a factor 2 of the addition-chain lower bound once its two trivial products (the first squaring of 1 and the first multiplication of 1 by a) are left out: (n - 1) + (popcount(e) - 1) <= 2(n - 1) <= 2 ceil(log2 e) for e >= 1; counting every executed multiplication, n + popcount(e) can exceed twice the bound (e = 2: 3 multiplications, bound 1). Methods with fewer multiplications: see background.
notes: Same doubling idea as fast doubling in fibonacci-naive-vs-dp. Modular exponentiation is the main step of the Miller-Rabin test in primality-miller-rabin-vs-aks (there through Python's built-in three-argument pow). Its role in public-key cryptography: see background.

background.statement: Window methods (2^k-ary, sliding window) need fewer multiplications than the binary method on long exponents.
Modular exponentiation is the basic operation of the RSA public-key cryptosystem and of Diffie-Hellman key exchange.
background.source: Rivest, Shamir, Adleman 1978; Diffie and Hellman 1976

background.statement: Machine-model assumption, not proved here: Python's bin(e) runs in time linear in the bit length of e. PROOFS.md, section 3, uses it for the cost of reading the bits.
